analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to pass pharmacy price concessions to pharmacies at the counter.
analysis.headline: The bill won 77 cosponsors from both parties but never got a committee vote before Congress ended, leaving pharmacy pricing rules unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare drug plans and their middlemen (pharmacy benefit managers) often negotiate a price with a pharmacy, then claw back part of it after the sale through retroactive fees and adjustments. This bill would require the full negotiated price to be paid at the point of sale, ban post-sale reimbursement cuts, require plans to reimburse pharmacies at least their cost of buying and dispensing the drug, and force detailed disclosure of every fee and adjustment on each claim. It also lets the government set standardized quality measures for pharmacy performance bonuses.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who fill prescriptions, who would see the true price of their drug at the counter, and community and independent pharmacies, which would stop losing part of their reimbursement to retroactive clawbacks and would get an objective, standardized system for any performance-based pay adjustments.

how_it_helps.text: Requires all negotiated price concessions, fees, and adjustments between a drug plan and a pharmacy to be included in the price paid at the point of sale starting in plan year 2020, so pharmacies and patients see the real price up front.

Bars plans and their contractors (including pharmacy benefit managers) from applying any post-sale incentive payments or adjustments that would decrease a pharmacy's reimbursement after the drug is dispensed, ending retroactive clawbacks.
Sets a floor: a plan may never pay a pharmacy less than the pharmacy's cost of purchasing and dispensing the drug.

Requires itemized, industry-standard claim-level disclosure of every fee, concession, and discount on the remittance advice, and requires an explanation if a plan's claimed negotiated price exceeds what it actually paid the pharmacy.
Prohibits the changes from increasing any beneficiary's cost sharing above what it would otherwise be.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare Part D drug plan sponsors, which currently keep a share of negotiated pharmacy prices through retroactive concessions and would have to pass that money back to pharmacies and disclose their pricing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: Plans currently use retroactive concessions to hold down premiums and negotiate lower net prices; passing those concessions through at the pharmacy counter could push plans to raise Medicare premiums or trim pharmacy networks to make up the money, a cost that would ultimately land on beneficiaries and taxpayers.

The detailed line-item disclosure and reimbursement floor requirements impose new administrative and compliance costs on plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers, which the industry argues raises program costs without directly lowering drug prices.

The bill requires an annual reconciliation-style check on whether the negotiated price exceeded actual reimbursement, but its remedy is only a written explanation from the sponsor, which critics would call weak enforcement for a transparency mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a well-documented complaint of community pharmacies: negotiated prices that shrink after the fact through fees and adjustments patients and pharmacies cannot see. In exchange, Medicare plans lose a tool they use to lower net costs, and some of that money may resurface in higher premiums. The transparency and no-clawback protections are real benefits for patients and pharmacies, and the bill carefully shields beneficiary cost sharing, but its enforcement mechanisms are mostly disclosure-based rather than penalty-based.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2019, with 77 cosponsors split between 18 House Democrats and 59 House Republicans.
It was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and no floor vote ever occurred in the two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors keep the retroactive price concessions they would have had to pass back to pharmacies and disclose, and no new transparency rules apply to their Medicare pharmacy pricing. Community pharmacies and Medicare patients got no relief from post-sale clawbacks. The outcome was likely helped along by a crowded PBM-reform field: committees weighed many competing drug-pricing bills that Congress and never scheduled this one for a vote. [S5, S1]

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug plan sponsors

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors
against.role: Insurance middlemen that administer Medicare drug plans
against.what_they_did: Lobbying groups for pharmacy benefit managers opposed point-of-sale pass-through mandates during this Congress, as such rules would end their retroactive pharmacy price concessions.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but Republican-leaning: 59 of 197 House Republicans and 18 of 231 House Democrats signed on, and the sponsor was a Republican; the bill never advanced far enough for a party-line floor vote.

industries.note: PBMs negotiate with pharmacies and take a slice of the negotiated price back through retroactive fees, concessions, and performance adjustments. The bill requires all of that money to show up in the price at the counter and bans post-sale reimbursement cuts, directly shrinking the middleman take.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurance plan sponsors
industries.note: Sponsors benefit from the retroactive concessions PBMs extract on their behalf and would have to pass those dollars through, disclose every pricing component on each claim, and pay pharmacies at least their acquisition cost. They would gain, however, from standardized quality measures replacing plan-by-plan pharmacy penalty systems.

These pharmacies are the direct beneficiary of the no-clawback rule and the reimbursement floor, which stops their payment from shrinking after the sale and guarantees they are paid at least their cost of the drug. Independent pharmacies operate on thin margins and have been the most vocal supporters of this kind of reform.

The bill directs the Secretary to define specialty pharmacies and tailor quality measures to their services, protecting high-cost drug dispensers from blanket incentive adjustments not relevant to their business.
